decisions.reason: The paper explicitly states in the Results section that it begins by replicating prior results on firm size and the likelihood of becoming an entrepreneur, citing Elfenbein et al. (2010) (listed in the References on page 17, lines 1080-1082 as Elfenbein DW, Hamilton BH, Zenger RZ, 2010, 'The small firm effect and the entrepreneurial spawning of scientists and engineers'). Both shipped and blind codings identify this target; the literal contiguous passage from the two-column layout is preserved verbatim.

decisions.quote:
For nondefunct firms, we replicate the
      “small-firm effect.” However, the small-firm effect no longer holds within the subsample of defunct firms: entrepreneurship
      rates among individuals present at firm dissolution are in fact higher for larger firms.
decisions.reason: The authors explicitly frame their test of the small-firm effect (Elfenbein et al. 2010) across nondefunct and defunct firms as yielding contrasting replication outcomes: they replicate the negative effect of firm size on entrepreneurship among nondefunct/all firms (Table 2, Column 1), but fail to replicate it—finding a statistically significant reversal—within the target subsample of defunct firms where internal career opportunities are extinguished (Table 2, Column 2; also summarized at Results, p. 12, lines 713-717 and Discussion, p. 15, lines 963-966). Under the codebook rules, when the authors' own overall synthesis presents the tested effect as replicating in the baseline sample and failing/reversing in the focal dissolved-firm test, the outcome is 'mixed'.

decisions.quote:
We test this claim in a setting where firm dissolution extinguishes internal opportunities, using a new hand-collected
      data set of career histories in the automatic speech recognition (ASR) industry. For nondefunct firms, we replicate the
      “small-firm effect.”
decisions.reason: The study collects and analyzes a new, hand-collected dataset of career histories in the automatic speech recognition (ASR) industry to re-test the previously published finding that smaller firms generate higher rates of entrepreneurship (the 'small-firm effect', including Elfenbein et al. 2010), making it a replication.
